rumours had spoken of madness, of bizarre experiments conducted in isolation, of strange lights seen at night, and of sudden, unexplained explosions. “Yes,” Aris said, his voice husky, the word a mere exhalation. “I remember. But… to manipulate the very fabric of reality, Grimal, to this extent. It beggars belief. What process, what unholy alchemy, could achieve such a thing?”

The distortion in the air pulsed again, a ripple like heat haze, only denser, more substantial. The hum intensified, a low, guttural vibration that seemed to emanate not from the air, but from within Aris’s own chest. It was an unsettling, visceral sound.

It was, as I said, a process. A culmination of years, Aris, years of theoretical work, followed by practical application, the most daring, the most profound experiment ever conceived.”

“You see, Aris, the conventional understanding of light and matter is fundamentally flawed, or at least incomplete. We perceive objects because they interact with light. They absorb certain wavelengths, reflect others, scatter yet more. My work focused on the refractive index, not merely as an optical property, but as a fundamental characteristic of matter itself. What if, I posited, one could so perfectly align the atomic structure of a body that light would pass through it unimpeded, without reflection, without absorption, without refraction, without even scattering?”

Aris frowned, his scientific mind, despite the horror, beginning to engage. “But that would require altering the very nature of the atoms themselves, their electron shells, their vibrational states. It’s an immense energy barrier. The body would cease to be itself. It would become something else entirely, a field, not matter.”

“Precisely, Aris, precisely!” Grimal exclaimed, a surge of energy in his voice that momentarily drowned the tremor. The hum intensified again, and the nebulous distortion in the air expanded perceptibly. It seemed to pulse rhythmically, like a gigantic, invisible heart. “Not a field, not exactly. But a state of matter so finely tuned, so perfectly attuned to the passage of electromagnetic radiation, that it becomes, for all intents and purposes, invisible. I discovered a particular spectrum of radiation, a precise frequency, that when applied to organic tissue, could induce a shift in the atomic and sub-atomic vibrational frequencies. It literally ‘tuned’ the atoms, Aris, to resonate at a rate that light simply ignored. Imagine a sieve, Aris, with holes precisely sized to let through only water, while holding back sand. My process was to make the ‘sieve’ of the body’s cells, its tissues, its very bones, perfectly transparent to light, allowing it to pass through as if nothing were there.”

Aris stared at the empty space where he knew Grimal was, his mouth slightly agape. The concept, though fantastical, was presented with such a terrifying, scientific precision that it sent a shiver down his spine. It was not magic; it was physics, pushed to its absolute, horrifying limit.

“But the energy,” Aris reiterated, his voice strained. “The energy required to sustain such a state. It would be monumental. And the stability? How could you maintain such a delicate equilibrium?”

“Ah, the crux of the matter, Aris, the very crux,” Grimal sighed, and the tremor returned, stronger now, a wavering quality to his voice. “The initial transformation was indeed an immense undertaking, a culmination of every joule I could generate in my isolated laboratory, a risk of such magnitude that any sane man would have recoiled. My body, having been tuned, maintained that tuning, much like a perfectly struck tuning fork vibrates for a time on its own. However, Aris, every system is subject to entropy. Every resonant frequency, without constant re-energization or perfect isolation, will eventually degrade. My body, living tissue, constantly metabolizing, regenerating, changing, is not a perfect system.”

The distorted patch of air pulsed violently, and Aris saw a faint shimmer ripple outwards from its center, like water disturbed by a falling stone. The low hum rose in pitch, becoming a distinct, high-frequency whine, grating on his nerves. He instinctively took a step back, bumping into the dressing table behind him.

My body is beginning to revert, not uniformly, but piecewise, chaotically. It is like a symphony, Aris, where the instruments begin to play out of tune, slowly at first, then more and more dissonantly, until all is cacophony. The stability I achieved is failing. The true, ruthless nature of the man, the relentless ambition that had driven him to such a state, was beginning to show itself.

“I cannot just walk into the university’s advanced physics lab and demand access to classified equipment,” Aris argued, trying to find a practical reason to refuse. “They would ask questions. They would never allow it. I’d be arrested.”

The threat, the sheer scientific audacity, the bizarre reality of the situation, it was all too overwhelming to simply dismiss. He was trapped.

“And the equipment for the shielding?” Aris asked, trying to buy time, to think. “How are we to improvise a Faraday cage?”

“Aluminium foil, Aris, and copper mesh, if you have it,” Grimal replied, his voice still rapid. “Common household items, in sufficient quantity. And then, once these immediate measures are in place, we will focus on the true solution, the university’s resources. But first, the compounds, and the cellar. Now, Aris, do not waste time. He was a man of science, a man of reason, thrust into a nightmare of impossible physics. He was afraid, profoundly so, but beneath the fear, a strange, undeniable flicker of scientific awe began to stir. To witness such a phenomenon, to be party to its very unraveling and potential re-stitching, it was beyond anything he could have imagined. It was less a voice and more a chorus of overlapping, distorted echoes. “I am… I am coming apart! Faster than I anticipated!”

The wallpaper behind the vortex was peeling, singed at the edges. Grimal’s disintegration was no longer a theoretical concept; it was a violent, destructive process affecting the very fabric of his surroundings.

“I have the compounds! I have prepared the cellar!” Aris shouted, his voice barely audible above the shriek and the strange, electrical crackling sounds now emanating from the vortex. “We must go now!”

It was, as I said, a process. A culmination of years, Aris, years of theoretical work, followed by practical application, the most daring, the most profound experiment ever conceived.”

Grimal paused, and Aris could almost sense a flicker of the old pride, the arrogant brilliance that had marked his university days, even amidst the present terror.

“You see, Aris, the conventional understanding of light and matter is fundamentally flawed, or at least incomplete. We perceive objects because they interact with light. They absorb certain wavelengths, reflect others, scatter yet more. My work focused on the refractive index, not merely as an optical property, but as a fundamental characteristic of matter itself. What if, I posited, one could so perfectly align the atomic structure of a body that light would pass through it unimpeded, without reflection, without absorption, without refraction, without even scattering?”

Aris frowned, his scientific mind, despite the horror, beginning to engage. “But that would require altering the very nature of the atoms themselves, their electron shells, their vibrational states. It’s an immense energy barrier. The body would cease to be itself. It would become something else entirely, a field, not matter.”

“Precisely, Aris, precisely!” Grimal exclaimed, a surge of energy in his voice that momentarily drowned the tremor. The hum intensified again, and the nebulous distortion in the air expanded perceptibly. It seemed to pulse rhythmically, like a gigantic, invisible heart. “Not a field, not exactly. But a state of matter so finely tuned, so perfectly attuned to the passage of electromagnetic radiation, that it becomes, for all intents and purposes, invisible. I discovered a particular spectrum of radiation, a precise frequency, that when applied to organic tissue, could induce a shift in the atomic and sub-atomic vibrational frequencies. It literally ‘tuned’ the atoms, Aris, to resonate at a rate that light simply ignored. Imagine a sieve, Aris, with holes precisely sized to let through only water, while holding back sand. My process was to make the ‘sieve’ of the body’s cells, its tissues, its very bones, perfectly transparent to light, allowing it to pass through as if nothing were there.”

Aris stared at the empty space where he knew Grimal was, his mouth slightly agape. The concept, though fantastical, was presented with such a terrifying, scientific precision that it sent a shiver down his spine. It was not magic; it was physics, pushed to its absolute, horrifying limit.

“But the energy,” Aris reiterated, his voice strained. “The energy required to sustain such a state. It would be monumental. And the stability? How could you maintain such a delicate equilibrium?”

“Ah, the crux of the matter, Aris, the very crux,” Grimal sighed, and the tremor returned, stronger now, a wavering quality to his voice. “The initial transformation was indeed an immense undertaking, a culmination of every joule I could generate in my isolated laboratory, a risk of such magnitude that any sane man would have recoiled. But I was not sane, not then, perhaps not now. I was driven. The transformation itself, once achieved, was self-sustaining for a time, a kind of resonant feedback loop. My body, having been tuned, maintained that tuning, much like a perfectly struck tuning fork vibrates for a time on its own. However, Aris, every system is subject to entropy. Every resonant frequency, without constant re-energization or perfect isolation, will eventually degrade. My body, living tissue, constantly metabolizing, regenerating, changing, is not a perfect system.”

The distorted patch of air pulsed violently, and Aris saw a faint shimmer ripple outwards from its center, like water disturbed by a falling stone. The low hum rose in pitch, becoming a distinct, high-frequency whine, grating on his nerves. He instinctively took a step back, bumping into the dressing table behind him.

“The process is decaying, Aris,” Grimal continued, his voice now laced with a raw, desperate urgency. “The harmonic frequency that sustains my invisibility, that holds my atoms in their precarious state, is breaking down. My body is beginning to revert, not uniformly, but piecewise, chaotically. It is like a symphony, Aris, where the instruments begin to play out of tune, slowly at first, then more and more dissonantly, until all is cacophony. The stability I achieved is failing. My cells, my tissues, they are losing their coherence, their perfectly aligned vibrational states. Some parts are becoming visible, then invisible again, then partially visible, then dissolving into a kind of energetic mist.”

Aris remembered the bloodstains, the way they had coagulated and become visible. This was the explanation. The horror of it was almost unbearable.

“And this… dissolution?” Aris managed to stammer, pointing a trembling finger vaguely at the swirling anomaly. “This is what happens when the frequency completely collapses?”

“In essence, yes,” Grimal confirmed, and the high-pitched whine from the distortion became sharper, more piercing. “My atoms are losing their structural integrity, their bonds weakening. My very being is scattering, Aris, dissipating into the surrounding environment. I am becoming less than matter, more than energy, an unstable quantum fluctuation. The ‘harmonic frequency’ I spoke of, it is the precise counter-frequency, the exact vibratory rate, that could restore stability, could re-tune my entire being. It would act as a kind of resonant dampener, locking my atoms back into their invisible, coherent state. But to generate such a frequency, Aris, with the necessary power and precision, it requires specific equipment, specific materials, and an immense surge of focused energy. And I am, at this moment, very much depleted. This,” he indicated the swirling blur, which now had a faintly metallic smell, like ozone after lightning, “is merely a symptom of my exhaustion, my struggle to maintain a semblance of cohesion.”

Aris felt a cold dread clamp around his heart. He was staring at a man who was literally coming apart at the seams of reality, and this man was asking for *his* help.

“But what can I do?” Aris asked, his voice barely audible above the rising whine. “I am a doctor, Grimal, not a physicist capable of manipulating sub-atomic structures. I have no such equipment, no such knowledge.”

“But you are a brilliant mind, Aris, a rational mind, and you have access,” Grimal retorted, the desperation now raw and palpable. The hum was now a persistent, headache-inducing shriek. “You know the university’s physics department, its laboratories. You know their resources, their specialists. I need specific apparatus, instruments capable of generating and focusing specific electromagnetic frequencies. A high-power resonant cavity, for one. And specific rare earth elements, doped crystals for a frequency modulator. Components that are not readily available on the open market, but which the university undoubtedly possesses, perhaps even in its research facilities. And, Aris, I need your brain, your critical thinking, your ability to make sense of my schematics, to verify my calculations.”

Aris shook his head, his mind reeling. “This is madness, Grimal. Even if I could access such equipment, what makes you think I could operate it, or even understand your designs?”

“You will understand, Aris, you must!” Grimal's voice was now sharp, edged with a rising hysteria. “I will guide you. My brain, though suffering, is still functioning. I have the designs, the formulas, the precise parameters. They are etched in my memory. But I cannot physically build, I cannot manipulate the controls, I cannot even reliably sustain myself in one location for long. I am a ghost, Aris, a dissolving phantom, dependent on a steady hand and a clear mind to anchor me back to reality. And you are that hand, that mind. You are my only hope.”

Aris could almost make out a vaguely human outline, a swirling vortex of nothingness where a body should have been. The air around it felt strangely cold, as if heat were being drawn into the anomaly.

“And if I refuse?” Aris asked, the words forced out, despite the knot of fear in his stomach. He knew the answer, or at least he feared it.

I cease to exist. And my unique, unparalleled knowledge, the secret of invisibility, the profound understanding of matter and light, it vanishes with me. Lost forever. The initial attempts at civility, the appeals to friendship, were wearing thin. The true, ruthless nature of the man, the relentless ambition that had driven him to such a state, was beginning to show itself.

You could arrange a consultation, a special project. Invent a plausible, if somewhat vague, reason. A study on unusual electromagnetic effects on biological tissue, perhaps? A new form of medical imaging? You are resourceful, Aris. You always were.”

“You expect me to lie, to steal, to risk my entire career, my reputation, for your… folly?” Aris burst out, the absurdity of the situation finally overcoming his terror for a moment.

“Folly?” Grimal’s voice sharpened, and the hum intensified to an almost unbearable level. “This is not folly, Aris! This is the greatest scientific achievement in human history! It is the unveiling of a new fundamental property of the universe! And you call it folly? You would let it, let *me*, dissolve into nothingness, simply because of your precious ‘career’?” A tangible wave of cold swept through the room, and the papers on Aris’s desk rustled as if in a sudden draft.

“I require certain preparatory steps first, Aris,” Grimal continued, ignoring Aris’s outburst. “My current state is too unstable even to begin formulating the full plan, the precise frequency calculations. I need energy, a stable environment, and a temporary measure to slow this disintegration. You fetched whiskey and food, a small comfort, but it is not enough. I need specific chemical compounds, metabolic regulators, to try and temporarily stabilize my cellular coherence. They are not difficult to acquire, common laboratory reagents. And I need a more confined, controlled space where the energy fluctuations from my body will not be quite so… disruptive.”

Aris looked around his bedroom, then at the pulsating, swirling anomaly. The walls seemed to vibrate with the high-pitched whine. He imagined Grimal’s disintegrating form, radiating these bizarre frequencies, warping the very fabric of the room. This was not a place for a delicate scientific endeavor, let alone for slowing the dissolution of a living being.

“What sort of compounds?” Aris asked, reluctantly, the question tasting like defeat. He knew, with a sinking certainty, that he was already drawn into Grimal’s mad scheme. The threat, the sheer scientific audacity, the bizarre reality of the situation, it was all too overwhelming to simply dismiss. He was trapped.

Grimal immediately launched into a string of chemical names and precise concentrations, delivered with the rapid-fire intensity of a man whose very existence hung in the balance. “Potassium iodide, a saturated solution, administered intravenously. A moderate dose of atropine sulfate, to regulate metabolic rate. And a powerful corticosteroid, dexamethasone, to reduce inflammation and stabilize cellular membranes. These are rudimentary, Aris, but they might buy us some time, slow the unraveling. And then, a chamber. An insulated, electromagnetically shielded chamber. Do you have one in your house? A Faraday cage, perhaps?”

Aris almost laughed, a hysterical, humorless sound. “A Faraday cage? In my house, Grimal? What do you take me for, a mad scientist?” He immediately regretted the jibe.

The whine intensified again, and a book on his bedside table, a weighty medical text, suddenly slid a few inches before thudding to the floor. The air crackled faintly.

“Do not provoke me, Aris,” Grimal warned, his voice dangerously low, almost a growl. “I am at my limit. If you do not have a dedicated chamber, then the most insulated, least frequented room in your house will have to suffice. A cellar, perhaps. Or a disused storage room, away from electronic interference. We will improvise the shielding.”

Aris considered. He had a small, unused wine cellar, rarely visited, deep beneath the house. It was cold, damp, and perfectly suited for isolation. “I have a cellar,” he admitted, his shoulders slumping. “It’s cold. And a bit dusty.”

“Excellent,” Grimal said, a note of triumph in his voice. “The cold will help slow the cellular processes, and the dust is inconsequential. Now, the compounds. You are a doctor, Aris. You have access to a surgery, a dispensary. These are common medical supplies. You can procure them, can you not?”

Aris knew he could. He had his own small practice, a well-stocked dispensary for emergencies. It would be easy enough to gather the items without suspicion. But the implications, the dark path he was being led down, weighed heavily on him.

“And the equipment for the shielding?” Aris asked, trying to buy time, to think. “How are we to improvise a Faraday cage?”

“Aluminium foil, Aris, and copper mesh, if you have it,” Grimal replied, his voice still rapid. “Common household items, in sufficient quantity. We will line the cellar, create a crude but effective shield against external electromagnetic noise. Every bit of stability helps. And then, once these immediate measures are in place, we will focus on the true solution, the university’s resources. But first, the compounds, and the cellar. Now, Aris, do not waste time. My atoms are singing a death knell.”

Aris swallowed, his throat suddenly dry. He looked at the swirling, shrieking anomaly, then at his own trembling hands. He was a man of science, a man of reason, thrust into a nightmare of impossible physics. He was afraid, profoundly so, but beneath the fear, a strange, undeniable flicker of scientific awe began to stir. To witness such a phenomenon, to be party to its very unraveling and potential re-stitching, it was beyond anything he could have imagined. It was monstrous, but it was also magnificent in its terrifying scope.

He moved towards the door, his legs feeling heavy, as if he were walking through thick mud. “I will get the compounds,” he said, his voice flat. “And I will prepare the cellar. But Grimal, this is insane.”

“Sanity is a luxury for those who are not dissolving, Aris,” the Invisible Man retorted, his voice chilling. “Now go. And do not, for a moment, think of alerting anyone. Remember, I can be anywhere, hear anything. And a desperate man has little left to lose, save his life.”

He felt a profound sense of isolation, of being utterly alone in a world suddenly turned upside down. The night was cold, but a deeper, more chilling cold had settled in his bones. He was now an accomplice, bound by fear and a morbid curiosity to a spectral, disintegrating being who had defied the very laws of nature. His life, he knew, would never be the same. He walked through his quiet house, the floorboards creaking under his uneasy tread, and descended the stairs towards his surgery, his mind already racing with the implications, the scientific impossibilities, and the terrible, undeniable reality of an Invisible Man.

He entered his small dispensary, the air thick with the scent of antiseptic and tinctures. His hands, still slightly shaking, moved almost automatically, selecting the vials and syringes Grimal had specified. Potassium iodide, atropine sulfate, dexamethasone. All readily available. He assembled a sterile kit, his medical training asserting itself even in this surreal situation. As he worked, his mind, despite the urgency, kept returning to Grimal’s explanation, dissecting it, seeking flaws, seeking any ray of hope that this might all be a delusion, an elaborate trick. But the swirling patch in his bedroom, the hum, the blood, the moved objects, all screamed otherwise. This was real.

He then made his way to the cellar. It was a small, brick-lined room, cool and dark, usually reserved for storing seldom-used household items and a few bottles of wine. He switched on the bare bulb hanging from the ceiling, its feeble light illuminating shelves laden with old trunks, dusty gardening tools, and forgotten boxes. He began to clear a space in the center, pushing aside objects with a frantic energy that belied his inner turmoil. The metallic tang of dust rose to his nostrils, mingling with the earthy smell of damp brick. This was to be Grimal’s sanctuary, his temporary anchor against the abyss. Aris shivered, not from the cold, but from the grim realization of what he was doing. He was building a nest for a dissolving ghost.

He spent the next hour ransacking his kitchen and tool shed for any materials that might serve as electromagnetic shielding. Rolls of aluminium foil, left over from cooking, were quickly gathered. He found an old, broken radio with a copper coil inside, which he carefully extracted. An old roll of chicken wire, surprisingly, also presented itself. It was crude, incredibly makeshift, but Aris, recalling Grimal’s desperate instructions, knew that any barrier, however imperfect, was better than none. He imagined the invisible particles of Grimal’s being, hemorrhaging energy, affecting everything around him, and the thought spurred him to greater haste.

Returning to the cellar, he began his bizarre task. He lined the walls, ceiling, and floor with layers of aluminium foil, taping it down with packing tape, creating a dull, shimmering cocoon. He then attempted to fashion a crude mesh screen from the chicken wire and the salvaged copper coil, intending to create a rudimentary Faraday cage around the central space. It was amateurish, certainly not scientifically rigorous, but it was the best he could do with the limited resources and time. The wine cellar, once a place of quiet storage, was transforming into something out of a science-fiction novel, a makeshift bunker for an impossible being.

As he worked, a new thought struck him, chilling him to the bone. If Grimal was truly disintegrating, if his atoms were scattering, what exactly was he breathing? What would become of his waste products? The very idea was grotesque, a scientific obscenity. He tried to push the thought aside, focusing on the immediate, tangible tasks.

It looked ridiculous, an amateur’s attempt at high-tech containment. But it was done. He gathered the medical kit, a jug of water, and a few blankets for Grimal, anticipating the cold. He hesitated at the cellar door, his hand on the rough wood. He was about to descend further into this madness, to become irrevocably intertwined with the fate of the Invisible Man.

As he approached the door, the low hum, which had seemed to recede during his frantic preparations, was now distinctly audible again, and it was louder, more urgent. The faint, metallic, ozone smell was stronger too. A sense of profound agitation emanated from behind the closed door. Grimal’s situation had clearly worsened.

The swirling anomaly was far larger now, a tumultuous vortex of indistinctness that seemed to almost fill the entire space between the bed and the wash-hand stand. It pulsated with a violent, erratic rhythm, and the high-pitched whine was now a deafening shriek, vibrating through the very floorboards. He could feel it in his teeth, his bones. Within the swirling chaos, flashes of light, almost like miniature lightning strikes, flickered and vanished. The air was thick with the scent of ozone and something else, something sharp and acrid, like burning flesh.

“Aris! You fool! What took you so long?” Grimal’s voice, though still distinct, was now fractured, interspersed with gasps and what sounded like sharp, involuntary cries of pain. It was less a voice and more a chorus of overlapping, distorted echoes. “I am… I am coming apart! Faster than I anticipated!”

Aris saw, with a fresh surge of horror, that the bedsheets were now not just bloodstained, but had dark, burned patches, as if subjected to intense, localized heat. The wallpaper behind the vortex was peeling, singed at the edges. Grimal’s disintegration was no longer a theoretical concept; it was a violent, destructive process affecting the very fabric of his surroundings.

“I have the compounds! I have prepared the cellar!” Aris shouted, his voice barely audible above the shriek and the strange, electrical crackling sounds now emanating from the vortex. “We must go now!”

“Help me, Aris!” Grimal cried, and Aris felt a sudden, searing pain in his arm. An invisible hand, no longer merely grasping, but digging in with desperate, claw-like intensity, had seized him. The grip was shockingly strong, almost bone-crushing, and radiated an unnatural coldness. The vortex seemed to lurch towards him, drawn by the contact.

“Don’t pull me in!” Aris gasped, trying to free himself, but Grimal’s grip was absolute. He was being dragged towards the swirling, shrieking void. The smell of burning intensified, and Aris felt his own skin begin to prickle and burn where Grimal’s hand gripped him.

“I am trying to cohere! You are my only anchor!” Grimal shrieked, and Aris saw, with a shudder, that the area of his arm directly beneath Grimal’s grip was beginning to shimmer faintly, its outlines blurring. He was being infected by the instability, or perhaps, simply being pulled into Grimal’s own chaotic field.

“Walk! Walk to the cellar!” Aris ordered, trying to maintain some semblance of control, despite his own rising panic. He stumbled forward, half-dragging, half-being-dragged by the invisible, disintegrating man. The vortex followed, a moving column of chaos, the shriek and crackle echoing through the house as they passed down the hall, then down the main staircase. Objects rattled on the walls, floorboards vibrated violently, and a vase on a landing table suddenly shattered, sending shards scattering.

The descent into the cellar was a horrifying ordeal. Grimal, still gripping Aris’s arm with agonizing force, seemed to be losing all bodily control. He would lurch, stumble, and then pull Aris along with him, his invisible form a constant source of violent, unpredictable movement. The searing cold, combined with the strange burning sensation, made Aris’s arm feel numb and agonizingly alive all at once. He could hear Grimal’s frantic, broken whispers, almost nonsensical, amidst the rising shriek, a litany of formulas and desperate pleas.

Finally, they reached the cellar. Aris, with a supreme effort of will, guided Grimal towards the makeshift copper-mesh cubicle he had prepared. The vortex, shrieking and sparking, seemed to compress as it entered the confined space, its intensity momentarily magnified. The aluminium foil walls shimmered and vibrated under the assault of Grimal’s energetic instability.

“Get in! Get into the mesh!” Aris cried, pushing Grimal forward.

With a final, almost inhuman shriek, Grimal stumbled, pulling Aris into the cubicle with him. The moment Grimal’s invisible, disintegrating form was fully inside the mesh, the shriek seemed to dull slightly, the crackling lessen. A profound, almost palpable sense of relief washed over Aris, despite the still-agonizing grip on his arm. The crude shielding was working, at least to some extent.

“Quickly, Aris! The injections!” Grimal gasped, his voice now a single, strained echo, though still laced with urgency. The hand gripping Aris’s arm relaxed slightly, though it did not let go.

Aris, his own arm throbbing with pain, fumbled for the medical kit. His hands were shaking so violently he almost dropped the syringe. He knew he had to act fast. He had to stabilize this spectral monster, not just for Grimal’s sake, but for his own sanity, his own survival. He was no longer just an observer; he was a participant, bound to the Invisible Man’s terrifying fate. He prepared the first syringe, drawing up the potassium iodide, his mind a whirlwind of scientific dread and a terrible, exhilarating wonder. The nightmare had only just begun.
